name: Hernia
definition: A hernia forms when muscle weakness lets tissue push through.
overview: Hernias are common, and most occur in the tummy or groin. Some cause a visible lump, while others are internal. Common types include inguinal (groin), femoral (top of the thigh), umbilical (belly button) and hiatus hernias, where part of the stomach moves up into the chest. Many cause few or no symptoms, but a trapped hernia can become a medical emergency.
causes: Muscle weakness that lets tissue push through.
Straining to poo, lifting heavy weights, coughing, pregnancy and losing weight very quickly.
For hiatus hernia the cause is not exactly clear, but the diaphragm weakening with age or pressure on the tummy may play a part.
riskFactors: Long-term constipation and straining to pass a stool.
Femoral hernias mainly affect women over 50, and inguinal hernias are more common in men.
signs: A bulge or lump that may get bigger on coughing or straining and smaller when lying down.
A small lump at the top of the thigh with a femoral hernia.
Redness over the hernia and signs of bowel obstruction when an inguinal hernia is trapped.
A soft swelling at the belly button with an umbilical hernia.
complications: Strangulation, when the blood supply to trapped tissue is cut off, which is a medical emergency.
Symptoms of intestinal obstruction such as bloating, nausea and vomiting.
Sepsis and gangrene after strangulation of an umbilical hernia.
Chronic pain in some people after repair surgery.
diagnosis: A GP can usually identify a hernia by examining the area. The doctor may ask the person to stand, cough or strain while checking for a bulge. Imaging such as ultrasound, CT or MRI is used when needed.
treatment: Treatment depends on the type of hernia, what caused it and whether it is new or has come back. Options include medicines for hiatus hernia indigestion, losing weight if overweight, and surgery to repair the hernia. If a hernia causes only a noticeable lump with no pain or discomfort, it is reasonable to keep an eye on it without planning an operation.
prevention: Triggers the NHS lists include straining to poo, lifting heavy weights, being overweight and coughing. For hiatus hernia symptoms, advice includes losing weight if overweight and stopping smoking.
seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for very bad tummy pain, being sick, being unable to pass wind or stools, a high temperature or sudden confusion. A bulge that is suddenly larger or no longer goes back in, redness, or sudden severe pain also needs urgent help from NHS 111 or a GP the same day, or 999 if severe. A GP appointment is the route for a suspected hernia that is not urgent.

sections.heading: What is a hernia and which types are there?
sections.body:
A hernia forms when muscle weakness lets tissue push through. Hernias are common, and most occur in the tummy or groin. Some cause a visible lump, while others are internal and cannot be seen from the outside.

An inguinal hernia appears in the groin and is diagnosed from the history and an examination of a lump there. A femoral hernia causes a small lump at the top of the thigh and mainly affects women over 50, although it can happen to anyone. An umbilical hernia is a soft swelling at the belly button. A hiatus hernia is different, because part of the stomach moves up into the chest. In many cases hernias cause no symptoms or very few.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a hernia?
sections.body:
The usual sign is a bulge or lump that may get bigger when the person coughs, sneezes or cries and smaller when they lie down. Many hernias cause little or no pain. Some hernias cause a visible lump, while others are internal, and in many cases there are no or very few symptoms. A femoral hernia can also cause aching around the lump and discomfort when walking. An umbilical hernia is usually painless, though in adults it can sometimes cause discomfort when coughing or straining.

Hiatus hernias typically cause heartburn, acid reflux, bloating, feeling sick, and difficulty or pain when swallowing. These are also the symptoms of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. A hiatus hernia does not normally need treatment if it is not causing problems.

sections.heading: What causes a hernia?
sections.body:
A hernia can form when muscle weakness lets tissue push through. The NHS lists straining to poo, lifting heavy weights, being overweight, coughing, pregnancy and losing weight very quickly among possible causes. MedlinePlus lists long-term constipation and straining, long-term coughing, extra weight, smoking and heavy exertion as contributors. It also notes that inguinal hernias are more common in men. Femoral hernias mainly happen in women over 50, but they can happen to anyone. Being overweight appears on both the NHS and MedlinePlus lists.

For hiatus hernias, it is not exactly clear what causes them. They may be due to the diaphragm weakening with age or pressure on the tummy. Umbilical hernias are common in babies and often resolve on their own.

sections.heading: How is a hernia diagnosed?
sections.body:
A GP can usually identify a hernia by examining the area. The doctor may ask the person to stand, cough or strain while checking for a bulge. Imaging such as ultrasound, CT or MRI is used when needed. NIDDK says an inguinal hernia is diagnosed from the history and an examination of a lump in the groin.

For a hiatus hernia, if stronger medicines do not work, a GP can send the person for tests. The NHS says to see a GP if a hiatus hernia causes symptoms that do not go away or pharmacy medicines do not help. For an umbilical hernia, the NHS advises seeing a GP if the lump is painful, hard, does not move, or is growing or not going away.

sections.heading: How is a hernia treated?
sections.body:
The treatment offered depends on the type of hernia, what caused it, and whether it is new or has come back. If a hernia causes only a noticeable lump with no pain or discomfort, it is reasonable to keep an eye on it without planning an operation. NIDDK says men whose inguinal hernias cause few or no symptoms may be able to delay surgery, but should watch for symptoms and see a doctor regularly. It also says most people with inguinal hernias will need surgery to repair them.

MedlinePlus adds that surgery is the only treatment that can permanently fix a hernia. For adults with an umbilical hernia, the NHS says surgery is recommended for most because the hernia is unlikely to get better by itself and the risk of complications is higher. Children usually do not need treatment for an umbilical hernia, which often disappears as they grow, though hospitals differ on timing.

sections.heading: What helps a hiatus hernia?
sections.body: A hiatus hernia is when part of the stomach moves up into the chest. Symptoms can include heartburn, acid reflux, bloating and difficulty or pain when swallowing. Most hiatus hernias need only lifestyle changes and medicines from a pharmacy. Common advice includes eating smaller meals, raising the head of the bed, losing weight if overweight, stopping smoking, cutting back on alcohol and avoiding trigger foods. Tight clothes around the waist are best avoided. Pharmacists may recommend medicines called antacids or alginates, which can help ease symptoms. Prescribed medicine should not be stopped without speaking to a doctor first. Surgery is usually a last resort, when other treatments have not worked and very bad symptoms continue.

sections.heading: When is a hernia an emergency?
sections.body:
The main danger is strangulation, when the blood supply to trapped tissue is cut off. This is a medical emergency, and a stuck or strangulated hernia needs emergency surgery. Signs include a bulge that is suddenly larger or no longer goes back in, fever, redness, sudden or severe pain or tenderness, and bloating, nausea and vomiting. The NHS femoral hernia page says to call 999 or go to A&E for very bad tummy pain, being sick, being unable to pass wind or stools, or a high temperature. Strangulation of an umbilical hernia can lead to serious conditions such as sepsis and gangrene.

Hiatus hernia symptoms that need urgent advice from NHS 111 or a GP the same day include weight loss without trying, difficulty swallowing, frequent vomiting, blood in vomit and upper tummy pain. For a non-urgent concern, the NHS says to see a GP if a hernia is suspected.

faqs.q: Can a hernia go away on its own?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Umbilical hernias are common in babies and often resolve on their own. In adults, the NHS says an umbilical hernia is unlikely to get better by itself, so surgery is recommended for most. A hiatus hernia does not normally need treatment if it is not causing problems.

No. Many hernias cause little or no pain, and an umbilical hernia is usually painless. Sudden or severe pain, tenderness, redness or fever can be a sign of strangulation, which is a medical emergency needing 999 or A&E.

Not necessarily. The NHS says a hernia that causes only a lump with no pain or discomfort can reasonably be watched without an operation. NIDDK says most people with inguinal hernias will need surgery, and MedlinePlus says surgery is the only treatment that permanently fixes a hernia.

It is a hernia where the blood supply to the trapped tissue is cut off. The NHS calls this a medical emergency. Warning signs include a bulge that is suddenly larger or will not go back in, severe pain, sickness and being unable to pass wind or stools. Call 999 or go to A&E.

faqs.q: Is a hiatus hernia the same as acid reflux?
faqs.a: No, but they are linked. A hiatus hernia is when part of the stomach moves up into the chest. Its symptoms, such as heartburn and acid reflux, are those of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease. A GP appointment is the route if symptoms do not go away or pharmacy medicines do not help.
